summary.case_overview: Writ Petition (Civil) 135 of 1970 was filed by His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru under Article 32 of the Constitution of India, challenging the constitutional validity of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 as amended [Page 1]. During the pendency of the petition, Parliament enacted the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971, the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971, and the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972 [Page 1] [Page 477]. A special Bench of 13 Judges was constituted to determine the extent of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368, the correctness of the majority decision in I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab, and the constitutional validity of the 24th, 25th, and 29th Constitutional Amendments [Page 1] [Page 71] [Page 375] [Page 426] [Page 470].
summary.facts_of_case: On March 21, 1970, the petitioner filed Writ Petition No. 135 of 1970 under Article 32 of the Constitution for the enforcement of his fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 25, 26, and 31, praying that the provisions of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 (Act 1 of 1964) as amended by the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969 (Act 35 of 1969) be declared unconstitutional and void [Page 1]. The Supreme Court issued rule nisi on March 25, 1970 [Page 1]. During the pendency of the writ petition, the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1971 (Kerala Act 25 of 1971) received Presidential assent on August 7, 1971, prompting the petitioner to file an application to urge additional grounds impugning its validity [Page 1]. In the interim, Parliament enacted the 24th, 25th, and 29th Amendments [Page 477]. By the 29th Amendment Act, 1972, the two Kerala land reform amendment Acts were included in the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 147] [Page 477]. The petitioner was subsequently permitted to amend his petition to challenge the constitutional validity of the 24th, 25th, and 29th Amendments [Page 477].
summary.legal_issues:
1. Whether the power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 is unlimited or subject to inherent and implied limitations preventing Parliament from altering or destroying the basic structure or essential features of the Constitution [Page 71] [Page 121] [Page 331] [Page 388].
2. Whether 'law' in Article 13(2) includes a Constitutional amendment passed under Article 368, thereby prohibiting the abridgement or taking away of Fundamental Rights under Part III [Page 7] [Page 71] [Page 153] [Page 375].
3. Whether the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971, amending Article 13 and Article 368, is constitutionally valid [Page 1] [Page 58] [Page 128] [Page 217] [Page 477].
4. Whether Section 2 of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971, substituting the word 'amount' for 'compensation' in Article 31(2), is constitutionally valid [Page 1] [Page 58] [Page 147] [Page 420] [Page 477].
5. Whether Section 3 of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971, inserting Article 31C to protect laws giving effect to Directive Principles under Article 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14, 19, and 31 and excluding judicial review through a declaration clause, is constitutionally valid [Page 1] [Page 64] [Page 109] [Page 141] [Page 242] [Page 369] [Page 477].
6. Whether the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972, inserting the Kerala Land Reforms Amendment Acts of 1969 and 1971 into the Ninth Schedule, is constitutionally valid [Page 1] [Page 71] [Page 147] [Page 204] [Page 477].
summary.important_arguments_or_content:
The petitioner argued that Parliament is a creature of the Constitution with limited amending power under Article 368 and cannot alter or destroy the essential features, basic elements, or fundamental principles of the Constitution, which belong to the sovereign people of India [Page 71] [Page 121] [Page 388]. Fundamental rights under Part III were argued to be natural, inalienable human rights that cannot be abrogated or emasculated by a constituted body [Page 45] [Page 280] [Page 343] [Page 489]. The petitioner further urged that Article 31C virtually delegitimizes the amending process under Article 368 by permitting ordinary legislatures to enact Constitution-breaking laws by simple majorities, overriding fundamental freedoms and completely excluding judicial review [Page 64] [Page 109] [Page 141] [Page 242] [Page 369].

The respondents (Union of India and State Governments) argued that the amending power under Article 368 is a plenary, unlimited constituent power containing no express, implied, or inherent limitations [Page 71] [Page 179] [Page 229] [Page 426]. They contended that the expression 'amendment' includes addition, variation, or repeal of any provision of the Constitution to adapt it to changing socio-economic needs and implement Directive Principles of State Policy [Page 166] [Page 198] [Page 267] [Page 413] [Page 483]. They argued that 'law' in Article 13(2) refers only to ordinary legislative laws and not to constituent amendments passed under Article 368 [Page 7] [Page 153] [Page 375] [Page 451].
summary.court_reasoning:
The Court evaluated the scope of Article 368 and overruled the majority view in Golak Nath case, holding that Article 368 contains both the power and procedure for amending the Constitution and that the word 'law' in Article 13(2) applies only to ordinary legislation, not to constitutional amendments made in exercise of constituent power [Page 7] [Page 115] [Page 147] [Page 153] [Page 204] [Page 375] [Page 451].

On the extent of the amending power, a majority of the Bench held that Article 368 does not enable Parliament to alter, destroy, or emasculate the basic structure or framework of the Constitution [Page 128] [Page 236] [Page 331]. Judges including Sikri C.J., Shelat, Grover, Hegde, Mukherjea, Jaganmohan Reddy, and Khanna JJ. held that while Parliament can amend any provision of the Constitution including fundamental rights, it cannot alter the basic features or essential elements of the Constitution [Page 71] [Page 128] [Page 236] [Page 331]. Khanna J. reasoned that the word 'amendment' postulates that the old Constitution survives without loss of its identity or basic structure [Page 331].

Regarding Section 2 of the 25th Amendment, the Court held that replacing 'compensation' with 'amount' in Article 31(2) is valid and that courts cannot review the adequacy of the amount fixed or determined, provided the amount is not completely illusory or arbitrary [Page 58] [Page 134] [Page 147] [Page 420] [Page 464].

Regarding Section 3 of the 25th Amendment (Article 31C), Sikri C.J., Shelat, Grover, Hegde, Mukherjea, and Jaganmohan Reddy JJ. held Article 31C invalid in whole or part due to delegation of constituent power and abrogation of fundamental rights [Page 64] [Page 109] [Page 141] [Page 255]. Khanna J. sustained the main provision of Article 31C but struck down the second part containing the declaration clause ('and no law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall be called in question in any court...'), holding that excluding judicial review strikes at the basic structure of the Constitution [Page 369]. Ray, Palekar, Mathew, Beg, Dwivedi, and Chandrachud JJ. found no implied limitations on Article 368 and upheld all the challenged amendments in full [Page 179] [Page 204] [Page 286] [Page 426] [Page 458] [Page 502].
summary.decision_or_conclusion:
The Supreme Court delivered its decision with the following main conclusions:
1. The majority view in Golak Nath's case is wrong; the power to amend the Constitution is located in Article 368, and 'law' in Article 13(2) does not include a constitutional amendment [Page 147] [Page 204] [Page 375].
2. The Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971 is valid [Page 58] [Page 128] [Page 147] [Page 204] [Page 426] [Page 486].
3. Article 368 does not enable Parliament to alter or destroy the basic structure or framework of the Constitution [Page 128] [Page 236] [Page 331].
4. Section 2 of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971 is valid [Page 58] [Page 147] [Page 204] [Page 242] [Page 426].
5. The first part of Article 31C (introduced by Section 3 of the Twenty-fifth Amendment) is valid subject to judicial review regarding whether a law has a direct and reasonable nexus with Article 39(b) or (c); the second part of Article 31C (the declaration clause excluding judicial review) is unconstitutional and void [Page 141] [Page 255] [Page 369] [Page 502].
6. The Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972 is valid [Page 71] [Page 147] [Page 204] [Page 426] [Page 502].
7. The writ petitions were remitted to the Constitution Bench to be determined in accordance with the judgment and the law [Page 71] [Page 502] [Page 2264].
summary.important_legal_provisions:
- Article 13 of the Constitution of India (laws inconsistent with or in derogation of fundamental rights) [Page 7] [Page 217] [Page 318] [Page 477].
- Articles 14, 19, and 31 of the Constitution of India (fundamental rights to equality, fundamental freedoms, and property) [Page 1] [Page 64] [Page 109] [Page 477].
- Article 31C of the Constitution of India (saving of laws giving effect to certain directive principles under Article 39(b) and (c)) [Page 64] [Page 109] [Page 141] [Page 242] [Page 369] [Page 477].
- Article 368 of the Constitution of India (power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and procedure therefor) [Page 7] [Page 115] [Page 217] [Page 477].
- Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971 [Page 58] [Page 147] [Page 217] [Page 477].
- Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971 [Page 58] [Page 64] [Page 147] [Page 477].
- Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972 [Page 71] [Page 147] [Page 204] [Page 477].
summary.simplified_explanation: In this historic judgment, the Supreme Court established the 'Basic Structure Doctrine' of the Indian Constitution [Page 128] [Page 236] [Page 331]. The Court decided that while Parliament has wide power under Article 368 to amend any provision of the Constitution, including fundamental rights, it cannot use this power to alter, destroy, or remove the basic framework or core features of the Constitution, such as democracy, secularism, and judicial review [Page 128] [Page 331] [Page 369]. Parliament can pass amendments to give effect to directive principles, but it cannot completely cut off the courts' power of judicial review to verify if a law actually serves those public purposes [Page 369] [Page 502].
